Choosing the number of clusters, and stability

Source: vignettes/articles/choosing-k.Rmd
choosing-k.Rmd

How many clusters are there? MosaiClusteR separates this question from the integration step: a method builds a dissimilarity and a hierarchy, and you choose k when you extract labels. This page shows how to pick k and how to check that the answer is stable.

k is chosen at label extraction

mosaic_labels(fit, k) cuts any fitted result into k clusters. You can try several values of k on one fitted result without re-running the integration:

library(MosaiClusteR)
data(mosaic_toy)
L <- mosaic_toy$List
fit <- SNF(L, type = "data", distmeasure = rep("euclidean", length(L)),
           normalize = rep(FALSE, length(L)), method = rep(list(NULL), length(L)))

lab3 <- mosaic_labels(fit, k = 3)
lab4 <- mosaic_labels(fit, k = 4)

Scoring a range of k

SelectnrClusters() scores a range of k with several criteria and returns one recommendation per criterion, as a one-row data frame. Reduce it to a single integer, for example by majority vote:

S  <- length(L)
sel <- SelectnrClusters(L, type = "data", distmeasure = rep("euclidean", S),
                        normalize = rep(FALSE, S), method = rep(list(NULL), S),
                        nrclusters = 2:6)
sel$Optimal_Nr_of_CLusters                 # one column per criterion

recs  <- as.integer(unlist(sel$Optimal_Nr_of_CLusters))
k_hat <- as.integer(names(sort(table(recs), decreasing = TRUE))[1])
k_hat

Treat the recommendation as a starting point, not a verdict. When criteria disagree, inspect the candidates directly rather than trusting the vote.

Sweeping and plotting

cluster_k_sweep() evaluates a fitted result across a range of k and returns a tidy data frame of silhouette and within-dispersion values, with the best k recorded as an attribute. cluster_selection_plot() draws the criterion against k so an elbow or a silhouette peak is easy to see.

sweep <- cluster_k_sweep(fit, k_range = 2:8)
sweep                                  # k, silhouette, within_dispersion
cluster_selection_plot(fit, k_range = 2:8, select = "elbow")

How to read them: the silhouette rises to a peak at the k that separates the objects best; the within-dispersion curve bends at an elbow where adding clusters stops paying off. A k that both criteria favour is a confident choice.

Cutting a fitted tree interactively

ChooseCluster() helps pick a cut height on a fitted hierarchy, which is useful when you want to see the tree before committing to a k.

Checking stability

A cluster count is more trustworthy when it survives perturbation. Two simple checks:

  • Across methods. Extract labels from several integration methods at the same k and compare them with cluster_agreement(). Structure that several paradigms agree on is more likely to be real.
  • Across resamples. Re-run a stochastic method (the M-ABC family, intNMF) with different seeds, or subsample the objects, and compare the resulting labels. High agreement means the solution is stable at that k.
labs <- list(
  ADC = mosaic_labels(ADC(L, distmeasure = "euclidean", normalize = FALSE), 3),
  SNF = mosaic_labels(fit, 3),
  ABC = mosaic_labels(M_ABC(L, NC = 3, seed = 1), 3)
)
# pairwise agreement between solutions at k = 3
outer(seq_along(labs), seq_along(labs),
      Vectorize(function(i, j) cluster_agreement(labs[[i]], labs[[j]])[["ARI"]]))

If the agreement is high across methods and across seeds, the k you picked is stable. If it drops, try neighbouring values of k and prefer the one whose structure reproduces.
